Peripheral neuropathies, by contrast, characteristically cause distal weakness accompanied by sensory loss, the feet and hands failing first while numbness or paraesthesia keeps company with the motor deficit. Because nerve conduction studies measure the amplitude, latency, and conduction velocity of signals travelling along peripheral nerves, those recordings show that markedly slowed nerve conduction velocity indicates demyelination of the peripheral nerve. By contrast, neurogenic disease produces large-amplitude, long-duration motor unit potentials, since surviving axons sprout to reinnervate orphaned fibres and so enlarge the territory of each motor unit. Fibrillation potentials on needle electromyography occur only in myopathy and never in neurogenic disease. On the evidence assembled, injury had befallen at least one of the two fibre populations, the motor axons or the sensory axons, and perhaps both populations alike.
